PART XXVI
The Nervous System

Chapter 611
Seizures in Childhood

DEFINITION
A seizure is a transient occurrence of signs or symptoms resulting from abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain. Febrile seizures are the most common seizure disorder of childhood, occurring in 2-5% of children between 6 months and 5 years of age.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
A simple febrile seizure is generalized, lasts less than 15 minutes, and does not recur within 24 hours. A complex febrile seizure is focal, lasts longer than 15 minutes, or recurs within 24 hours. The child is typically neurologically normal before and after the event.

DIAGNOSIS
Lumbar puncture should be strongly considered in any child younger than 12 months presenting with a first febrile seizure, and in any child with meningeal signs. Routine electroencephalography and neuroimaging are not indicated after a simple febrile seizure in a neurologically normal child.

TREATMENT
Most febrile seizures are self-limited. For a seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes, give midazolam 0.2 mg/kg intranasally or buccally, maximum 10 mg per dose. Alternatively give rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg, maximum 20 mg per dose. Continuous prophylactic anticonvulsant therapy is not recommended for simple febrile seizures.

PROGNOSIS
Approximately 30% of children who have one febrile seizure will have a recurrence. The risk of subsequent epilepsy after a simple febrile seizure is approximately 1%, only marginally above the population baseline.

Chapter 612
Bacterial Meningitis Beyond the Neonatal Period

ETIOLOGY
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis account for the majority of cases in children beyond the neonatal period in populations with routine Haemophilus influenzae type b immunization.

TREATMENT
Empiric therapy is ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours, maximum 4 g per day, plus vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 2-4 days may be considered, given before or with the first dose of antibiotic.

PART XV
Infectious Diseases

Chapter 220
Acute Otitis Media

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
Acute otitis media presents with a bulging tympanic membrane, otalgia, and fever. Otorrhea of acute onset not attributable to otitis externa is also diagnostic.

TREATMENT
First-line therapy is high-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours for 10 days in children younger than 2 years. For children with recent beta-lactam exposure or concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, use amoxicillin-clavulanate. Observation without antibiotics for 48-72 hours is an option in children older than 2 years with non-severe unilateral disease and reliable follow-up.
